name: Backstage Bleed
definition: Present when any user-facing string contains an internal identifier — a template key, variable name, enum value, or interpolation syntax — instead of the human-readable value it stands for.
symptom: Machine vocabulary appears where a human word should be.
fix_pattern: Map every internal key to a display label at the boundary; lint for interpolation syntax, snake_case, and known enum tokens in rendered copy.

other.citation: NN/g #2 Match between system and the real world (Jakob Nielsen, nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: A template renders 'No category-code items in this collection yet,' exposing an implementation key as user-facing copy.

name: Counted in Crates
definition: Present when a displayed count tallies a different unit than the one the surrounding copy or the user's task implies (containers counted, contents claimed, or vice versa).
symptom: The number is technically true and humanly false.
fix_pattern: Count in the unit the label names; if the unit must differ, change the label to name what is actually counted.

other.citation: NN/g #2 Match between system and the real world (Jakob Nielsen, nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)
GOV.UK style guide A-Z: numbers

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: a count tallied parent groups while the surrounding task and labels described saved items.

name: Arithmetic Mirage
definition: Present when numbers visible on one screen fail their own arithmetic — a '+N more' indicator, subtotal, or badge that contradicts the visible items or the stated total.
symptom: The overflow badge and the visible items do not add up to the set.
fix_pattern: Derive overflow counts from the same source as the total (total minus visible), never from a second query or a hardcoded value.

other.citation: NN/g #2 Match between system and the real world (Jakob Nielsen, nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)
GOV.UK style guide A-Z: numbers

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: a remainder label repeated the total instead of subtracting the visible cards.

name: Phantom Freshness
definition: Present when metadata copy asserts a data-dependent fact (latest data, last updated, sync status) about an entity that contains no data, or when the assertion contradicts an adjacent zero-count on the same line.
symptom: An empty thing claims to be fresh.
fix_pattern: Gate data-dependent metadata behind a data-exists check; empty states get empty-state copy, not vitals.

other.citation: NN/g #2 Match between system and the real world (Jakob Nielsen, nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: an empty object claimed recent data despite having no data, and mixed date formats in the same line.

name: Scolding Machine
definition: Present when error copy blames the user, performs apology, or exposes machine internals — any of: 'you forgot', 'sorry', 'oops', 'please', 'valid'/'invalid', or a raw error code shown as the message.
symptom: The error talks about fault or internals instead of the fix.
fix_pattern: State what happened and what to do next in neutral, specific terms; keep codes in logs, not copy.

other.citation: GOV.UK error message component: banned words documented verbatim
Apple HIG alerts: never title an alert 'Error'
NN/g #9 Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors (Jakob Nielsen, nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: 'error 0x0000000643' or 'you forgot to enter' — GOV.UK bans both patterns explicitly.

name: Foghorn Error
definition: Present when an error message could be pasted onto any other error in the product without losing accuracy — it names neither the item in error, the cause, nor a next step.
symptom: Loud that something is wrong, silent about what and where.
fix_pattern: One message per failure mode: name the field or object, the condition violated, and the corrective action.

other.citation: GOV.UK error message component: bans 'An error occurred' and 'This field is required'
NN/g #9 Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors (Jakob Nielsen, nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)
Shneiderman #5 Prevent errors

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: 'An error occurred' and 'This field is required' — both documented GOV.UK catch-all bans.

name: Blindfold Link
definition: Present when a link's text, read alone out of context, does not identify its destination or purpose — e.g. 'click here', 'more', 'learn more', a bare 'here'.
symptom: A list of the page's links reads as noise.
fix_pattern: Front-load the link with the destination's own terms; the link text should survive being read in isolation.

other.citation: WCAG failure technique F84
GOV.UK writing guidance: front-load links with relevant terms

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: 'click here' / 'more' as link text — WCAG failure F84.

name: Blank Doorplate
definition: Present when a page title, dialog header, or section label is generic or hardcoded where a specific, contextual name is available — the title does not distinguish this page or state from its siblings.
symptom: The header describes the category of the thing, not the thing.
fix_pattern: Compute the title from the same state the view renders; if the code knows the noun, the header uses it.

other.citation: WCAG failure technique F25
Apple HIG: name the action, not the abstraction

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: a modal header used a hardcoded object name while the same view computed the correct context-specific noun.

name: Painted-On Headings
definition: Present when text styled to look like a heading is not marked up as one, or when heading levels skip (an h2 followed by an h4) so the document outline no longer matches the visible structure.
symptom: Looks structured to the eye, flat or scrambled to a screen reader.
fix_pattern: Mark up every visual heading with the semantic level its position implies; style the tag, never fake the tag with styling.
illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: visual headings used plain spans and skipped semantic levels, leaving no equivalent hierarchy for assistive technology.

name: Corporate Fog
definition: Present when interface prose exceeds roughly a 25-word sentence, uses passive voice where an actor exists, or uses an abbreviation before explaining it.
symptom: The user re-reads a sentence to find out what to do.
fix_pattern: One idea per sentence, active voice, age-9 reading level; expand every abbreviation on first use.

other.citation: GOV.UK writing guidelines: sentence length, reading age, active voice (note: WCAG 3.1.x cites are AAA, not a legal baseline)

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: Sentences past the ~25-word ceiling and unexplained abbreviations — both against GOV.UK writing guidance.

name: Guessing-Game Field
definition: Present when an input expects user data but provides no visible label or instruction stating what is expected, including any required format.
symptom: The user's first attempt at the field is a guess.
fix_pattern: Every input gets a persistent visible label plus format hints where format matters; placeholder text is not a label.

other.citation: GOV.UK form design guidance

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: Input expected with no label or instruction — WCAG 3.3.2 failure.

name: Echo Interrogation
definition: Present when the same information is asked of the user more than once within a single process without being auto-populated or selectable from the earlier answer.
symptom: The form asks a question the product was already told.
fix_pattern: Carry earlier answers forward as prefilled or selectable values; re-ask only for security confirmation.
illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: Asked twice for the same info in one process — WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, new in WCAG 2.2.

name: Needless Census
definition: Present when a form collects identity data (gender, sex, title, ethnicity) that the service does not demonstrably need, or offers option sets too narrow for the people answering, or asks without explaining why.
symptom: A personal question with no stated purpose and no room to answer truthfully.
fix_pattern: Only ask if genuinely needed, say why, offer inclusive options plus a self-describe or prefer-not-to-say path.

other.citation: GOV.UK design system: 'Gender or sex' pattern — only ask if genuinely needed, explain why

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: Self-identification fields offering needless or narrow options — the case GOV.UK's gender/sex pattern exists to prevent.

name: Silent Picture
definition: Present when informative imagery has no text alternative or a noise alternative (filename, 'image'), when decorative imagery is announced instead of hidden, or when text is rendered as an image where real text would serve.
symptom: What the image says is unavailable to anyone not looking at it.
fix_pattern: Alt text states the image's function in context; decorative images get empty alt; text ships as text.
illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: Alt text absent or decorative-noise (1.1.1); images of text where styled text was possible (1.4.5).

name: Patchwork Voice
definition: Present when the same content fact or convention — a person's identity, a date format, a capitalization rule, a tone register — appears in two conflicting forms within one product surface.
symptom: The product disagrees with itself about its own facts and style.
fix_pattern: One source of truth per fact and per format convention; seed/mock data defined once and imported, never re-declared per component.

other.citation: GOV.UK style guide A-Z: dates

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: adjacent components represented the same person with conflicting names, initials, roles, and date formats.

name: Yesterday's Signage
definition: Present when copy describes a feature, name, limit, or behavior that no longer matches the shipped product, or references a destination that no longer exists.
symptom: The words describe the product as it used to be.
fix_pattern: Treat copy as code: every behavior change ships with a grep for prose that described the old behavior.

other.citation: GOV.UK content guidance: review and retire outdated content
NN/g #2 Match between system and the real world (Jakob Nielsen, nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)

illustration: Non-evidentiary illustration: Outdated claims, dead references, and copy describing features that changed.
